name: Mbunga
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 14 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de doctorat d'État, Université Paris V René Descartes (theses.fr 1992PA05H011). DDL Lyon PDF edition, 542 pp.
catalog_quote: e) perte des oppositions prosodiques BC: nyoro-tooro, certains sous-dialectes nyankore (groupe III); nyakyusa (groupe X); tumbuka, sena (groupe XII); wanji ?, kisi ? (groupe XV); pogolu, ndamba, mbunga (groupe XVI); swahili (groupe XVIII) [p. 461]. a) langues à culmination de longueur et de hauteur sur la pénultième (langues sans prosodèmes distinctifs, ni opposition de longueur): tumbuka, sena; kisi ?; pogolu, ndamba et mbunga; nkwele, doe, zalamo, kutu, kami; plusieurs dialectes swahili; [p. 483]. Finalement, le stade V regroupe les langues sans oppositions prosodiques, qui sont toutes à accent démarcatif pénultième [p. 488].

new_statements.translation: e) loss of the Common Bantu prosodic oppositions: ... pogolu, ndamba, mbunga (group XVI); swahili. a) languages with culmination of length and pitch on the penultimate (no distinctive prosodemes, no length opposition): ... pogolu, ndamba and mbunga ... Finally, stage V comprises the languages without prosodic oppositions, all of which have a penultimate demarcative accent.

new_statements.relation_note: Mbunga (with Pogolo and Ndamba) has lost the Proto-Bantu prosodic oppositions; it is a language without distinctive prosodemes or length opposition, with culmination of length and pitch on the penultimate (demarcative penultimate accent).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No distinctive tone; demarcative accent (length and pitch peak) on the penultimate syllable of the word.
new_statements.identity_note: grouped with pogolu G51 and ndamba G52 as 'XVI (Kilombero)', Guthrie P15 = Mbunga of Ifakara; own field notes (p. 515 'pogolu, ndamba, mbunga (groupe XVI)') [name in source: mbunga (P 15) (groupe XVI Kilombero); pages 73 (Tableau 1), 77 (Tableau II), 461 (3.1 e), 483 (3.5.2a), 499 (3.6.1), 515 (Sources)]

sources.citation: Bernander, Rasmus, Eva-Marie Bloom Ström & Hannah Gibson. 2022. Post-verbal negative particles in Southern Tanzania: form, distribution and historical development. Africana Linguistica 28: 55-113 (Helda open reprint).
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Mbunga (P15) data come only from David Odden's field notes (p.c. 2021) and are called 'rudimentary' (fn. 9); quotes Nurse (1988:40): 'Mbunga today is phonologically a member of Rufiji-Ruvuma [N10, P10-P20], lexically more similar to Kilombero [G50]'. Confirms no grammar/phonology of Mbunga is available to specialists.

sources.note: Catalogue only: lists Glottolog, Ethnologue and LINGUIST List entries; no language description, no lexical or text resources.

sources.citation: Odden, David. n.d. 'My Languages: the languages I've worked on' (Odden Linguistics website) — lists 'Kimbunga [Tanzania]' and 'Chipogolo [Tanzania]' among fieldwork languages; the underlying unpublished Kimbunga field notes are the ones cited as 'Odden p.c. 2021' in Bernander, Ström & Gibson 2022.
sources.note: No linguistic content on Kimbunga is posted (site holds Logoori grammar/dictionary/texts, North Saami, teaching material). Confirms that primary Kimbunga data collected by a Bantu tonologist exist offline; obtaining a statement requires asking Odden (human step).

sources.citation: Lewis, M. Paul, Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig (eds.). 2015. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 18th edition. Dallas: SIL International. Entry 'Mbunga [mgy]' (Internet Archive copy 2019-06-05).
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology/typology field at all. Content: Alternate Names Bunga, Kimbunga; Population 29,000 (1987); Language Status 6b; Classification P, Matuumbi (P.15); 'Dialects: None known. Lexical similarity: 69% with Ndamba [ndj], 57% with Pogolo [poy]'; 'Writing: Unwritten'; 'Other Comments: There may be 2 varieties called Mbunga, each classified somewhat differently.' No language-development resources or survey report cited.

sources.citation: Odden, David. 2003. Rufiji-Ruvuma (N10, P10-20). In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 529-545. London: Routledge.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: p.529 mentions Mbunga only for classification (assigned to P10 by Guthrie; Nurse 1988:36-40). Sec. 2.3 Tone, p.534: 'All P-zone languages are tonal (though Ndengereko is losing distinctive prosody under Swahili influence)' -- a zone-level generalisation; the chapter's data are Matuumbi, Yao, Makonde plus Mwera/Ngindo/Ndengereko field notes, no Mbunga prosodic data. No word-stress statement for Mbunga.

sources.citation: Nurse, Derek & Gérard Philippson. 1975 [CLDF edition 2019, lexibank/tls, ed. R. Forkel et al.]. Tanzania Language Survey: wordlists 'Mbunga' (978 items) and 'Kimbunga' (983 items). cldf/.
sources.note: No phonology content: 1,961 lexical forms in plain roman orthography; a character census finds zero non-ASCII characters (no tone diacritics, no length marks, no stress marks), so the TLS transcription gives no prosodic evidence for Mbunga either way.

sources.citation: Brantschen, P. Anastas (OFMCap). 1953. Die ethnographische Literatur über den Ulanga-Distrikt, Tanganyika-Territorium. Acta Tropica 10(2): 150-185.
sources.note: Nothing on the language itself. The only linguistic work recorded for the district is Hendle 1907, a Pogoro grammar ('Die Ergebnisse seiner Sprachforschung veröffentlichte P. Hendle in einer Grammatik der Pogorosprache (44)'); for the Mbunga the author states that far less material exists than for the Pogoro and lists only historical, catechetical and ethnographic notes (Käppeli, Lussy, Damm, Culwick). Confirms that no missionary grammar/vocabulary of Kimbunga existed by 1953.
